I have been working this land for 30 years. I know this soil. I know what Quzhou weather does. My father farmed before me and I learned by watching and doing, not from any school. My two kids have taken jobs in the city so it is mostly my wife and me doing the field work, with help at harvest time.

I have 10.9 mu total. I keep 8 mu in the wheat-maize rotation — that is my stable income, the thing I can count on. The other 2.9 mu I put in cotton. Cotton is harder and the price has been uncertain these past years, but I know how to grow it and it brings in different income so I do not put all my risk in one crop.

For wheat I will sow in October after I pull the maize. I will do rotary tillage to chop up the stalks and work them in, then sow. I use the improved wheat seed I buy from the county seed store — the same variety I have used for three or four years now, it suits our land. I will water four times: once before sowing to get good germination, once in winter to protect the roots from the cold, once at jointing, and once during grain filling. I put down urea in two goes — base fertilizer before sowing and topdressing at jointing. I spray for aphids and powdery mildew, two rounds usually.

For summer maize I sow right after wheat harvest in June. I use hybrid seed, everyone around here uses hybrid now, it is clearly better. I seed directly without tillage — the wheat stubble is still there but I just drill in. I water three times and fertilize mostly with urea at planting and again around the big bell stage. Two pesticide rounds — one for weeds early and one for corn borer if needed.

For cotton I prepare the plot in March with a plough to get it deep and loose, then ridge it. I transplant in late April or early May using seedlings I raise in plastic film nurseries — I have done this every year. Cotton needs the most attention: I water four times, I spray five times because of bollworm and whitefly, and I top the plants once to control height. It is the most labor-intensive thing I grow.
